At 3:17 every morning, the moon rang the doorbell.

Not loudly. It pressed once, waited, then pressed again with the patient courtesy of someone who knew they were expected.

Mara would wake beneath the blue-gray quilt, listen to the chime traveling through the house, and stare at the ceiling until the sound faded. She never went downstairs. She never looked through the peephole.

Her mother had taught her better.

“Some things,” her mother used to say, “only knock when they want to be let in.”

The first time it happened, Mara was six. Her mother had been alive then, sitting beside the bed and reading from a book with no title on its spine. Outside, rain scratched at the window. Inside, the house smelled of cinnamon and dust.

The bell rang.

Mara sat up. “Who is it?”

Her mother closed the book.

“No one you know.”

“Should we answer?”

“Absolutely not.”

Then she tucked the quilt beneath Mara’s chin and stayed until morning.

After that, the moon came every night.

Years passed. Mara’s mother disappeared in the ordinary way people disappear from houses: first her voice, then her slippers, then the dent in the armchair. One day Mara came home from school and found the front door open. The kettle was boiling. The book lay face down on the kitchen table.

Her mother was nowhere.

The police asked questions. Neighbors brought casseroles. A man with a clipboard suggested that grief could make a person imagine patterns where none existed.

But the moon kept ringing.

Now Mara was thirty-two and lived alone in the same house, though the wallpaper had faded and the garden had turned to weeds. She worked at the town archive, where she catalogued things people had forgotten they owned: letters, wedding portraits, keys to vanished doors.

At lunchtime, she found a photograph tucked inside a box labeled MISCELLANEOUS.

It showed her mother standing in front of the house.

Except the house was different. Newer. Smaller. And behind her mother, on the porch, stood a girl in a yellow coat.

Mara knew that coat.

She had worn it when she was six.

On the back of the photograph, in her mother’s handwriting, were seven words:

SHE WILL COME WHEN YOU ARE READY.

That night, Mara sat at the kitchen table until 3:16.

At 3:17, the bell rang.

Once.

Twice.

Mara stood.

The house seemed to hold its breath. Floorboards creaked beneath her feet as she crossed the hall. Dust floated in the moonlight. She reached the front door and placed her hand on the knob.

On the other side, someone whispered her name.

Not Mara.

The name her mother had used when she was small. A private name, made of soft syllables and nonsense, something that belonged to bedtime and fever and the warm hollow beneath a parent’s arm.

Mara unlocked the door.

The porch was empty.

Above the roof, enormous and pale, the moon hung low enough to touch. Its surface was not stone but water, rippling with reflected stars.

Then the girl in the yellow coat stepped out from behind the lilac bushes.

She was six years old.

She looked exactly as Mara remembered herself: two missing teeth, one untied shoe, a smear of jam on her sleeve.

“Are you my mother?” Mara asked.

The girl shook her head.

“Are you me?”

Another shake.

She reached into her coat pocket and pulled out a small brass key.

Mara recognized it. Her mother had worn it around her neck on a red thread. Mara had once asked what it opened.

“Something important,” her mother had said.

The girl held out the key.

Behind her, the front door of the house stood open—not the house Mara knew, but the house from the photograph. Its windows glowed gold. Someone inside was humming.

Mara took the key.

The girl turned and walked toward the doorway.

For the first time in twenty-six years, Mara heard her mother’s voice.

“Mara,” it called, warm and impatient. “Come in before it gets cold.”

Mara looked back at the house she had lived in all her life: the peeling walls, the dead garden, the kettle that had never stopped waiting.

Then she stepped across the threshold.

The door closed behind her.

At 3:18, the moon stopped ringing.

And in a town where everyone had forgotten how to dream, a little girl in a yellow coat walked home carrying a woman’s hand.
